cameron-boozer: Boozer walked into the best situation of anybody in this class. Memphis handed him the keys to the frontcourt from day one and he looked ready for it in Vegas, making All-Summer League First Team at 18.5 points, 8 boards and nearly 4 assists a night. The feel and polish are what jump out. He processes the game faster than guys three years older. The knock has always been that he's more skilled than explosive, so watch whether he can create separation against NBA length. As a dynasty asset, he's the safest bet in the class and the usage is already there.
darryn-peterson: The Jazz took Peterson at two and immediately put the offense in his hands. He torched Salt Lake City summer ball at 26.5 a game on ridiculous shooting splits, then had a messier Vegas debut with 24 points but eight turnovers, which is really the whole scouting report in one line. Elite scoring gravity, still learning to run a team. Utah has zero reason to slow-play him, so the leash will be long and the counting stats should pile up. The efficiency will lag early. The asset value is top shelf.
aj-dybantsa: The number one pick landed in Washington, which is the one thing keeping him from being the consensus top rookie asset. The Wizards have young wings everywhere, so his usage won't be handed to him the way Boozer's was in Memphis. The talent is not in question. He averaged 25 in limited summer league run and guards multiple spots with real athleticism. Long term he might still end up the best player from this draft. Short term, expect some nights where the shot distribution frustrates you. Buy the dip if his managers get impatient.
caleb-wilson: Wilson announced himself with 35 in his Vegas debut, the second biggest scoring night in a summer league debut since they started tracking. Chicago sees him as a wing rather than a four, and the motor and defensive tools are legit. The Bulls have minutes to give, so the runway is real. What needs work is the jumper. If the three falls consistently he outplays his draft slot, if it doesn't he's a high-energy role guy for a while. Nice blend of floor and upside as an asset.
keaton-wagler: Wagler started summer league slow, then the second half of his second game showed why the Clippers took him at five. He's at his best surrounded by shooting, moving the ball and picking apart rotations. That's also the catch, because LA's roster is veteran-heavy and nobody is clearing a lane for a rookie guard. Expect a modest role early with the fantasy payoff coming later. He needs to add strength and prove he can create against pressure. Patience asset, but a smart front office picked him for a reason.
mikel-brown: Brooklyn at six is about as much runway as a young point guard can ask for. Brown is a shifty, creative ball handler who gets anywhere he wants on the floor, and the Nets have no reason not to let him play through every mistake. The frame is the issue. He needs NBA strength before he can finish through contact consistently, and the defense will be a problem early. In dynasty terms he's a classic rebuild asset: ugly efficiency now, real lead-guard equity later.
darius-acuff: Sacramento grabbed Acuff at seven and he fits the mold of guards who score first and figure out the rest later. He's a tough shot maker with deep range and real wiggle off the dribble. The Kings' backcourt has openings, so the opportunity should come quickly. What he has to clean up is shot selection and reading the floor when defenses load up on him. If the playmaking develops he's a starter, if not he's instant offense off the bench. Worthwhile asset either way at his price.
kingston-flemings: Flemings might have been the most quietly impressive rookie in Vegas. Fourteen assists against two turnovers across his first two games, plus five steals and three blocks, which is absurd defensive playmaking from a point guard. Atlanta got a floor general who makes everyone else's life easier. The reason he went eighth and not higher is the scoring. The pull-up is a work in progress and teams will go under screens until he punishes them. Assist-heavy formats should value him a tier above where most rankings have him.
brayden-burries: Milwaukee needed backcourt youth badly and Burries gives them a bucket-getter to grow. He scores at all three levels and plays with an edge that older Bucks teams have been missing. The concerns are the same ones from his Arizona tape: he hunts his own shot first, and the efficiency dips when the defense makes him a passer. His role should grow all season on a roster that needs what he does. Solid mid-round rookie asset with sneaky scoring upside.
hannes-steinbach: Steinbach is the kind of big whose value shows up on winning plays more than box scores, though the boards come in bunches. Relentless motor, screens hard, runs the floor, keeps possessions alive. That translates fast at the NBA level and coaches trust it, so he could carve out rotation minutes before flashier rookies do. The ceiling question is about range and rim protection, because right now he's between roles defensively. In deeper leagues the rebounding floor alone makes him rosterable early.
aday-mara: A legit 7-3 with soft hands and touch, Mara is the classic size bet. Fantasy-wise the blocks and lob finishes will come whenever he's on the floor, and Michigan showed his passing is better than people assume for his size. The whole question is whether his body lets him play NBA minutes, because mobility and conditioning have chased him his entire career. If he sticks in a rotation he's a per-minute monster. Stash asset with a real chance to matter in category leagues.
yaxel-lendeborg: The Summer League MVP nobody saw coming. Lendeborg went 19-5-6 in his debut and just kept stacking productive games as a do-everything connector forward. He's an older rookie, which caps the dynasty shine, but older rookies with his skill level tend to grab real minutes fast because coaches can trust them. He rebounds, passes and defends multiple spots. The three-point volume needs to grow for him to be a full-time starter. Great value asset for contenders who want production now instead of promise later.
nate-ament: Ament is a smooth 6-9 forward who gets shots off at a size that always finds a home in this league. The shot-making is genuinely pretty, turnaround jumpers and clean mechanics from deep. What holds him back right now is strength and the consistency of it all, because he can disappear for stretches when the physicality ramps up. Typical year-one arc: flashes, then a wall, then a real role in year two. Buy him as a patience asset before the flashes do their thing to his price.
morez-johnson: Dallas took Johnson at nine for the toughness. He's a bruising interior athlete who rebounds out of his area, sprints the floor and finishes everything around the rim with bad intentions. That skill set gets on NBA floors early because every rotation needs it. The offensive game outside five feet is still theoretical, and the free throws need serious work, which caps him in some category formats. Points-league managers can be more aggressive. Reliable big-man floor, modest ceiling unless the touch develops.
cameron-carr: The Lakers might have gotten the steal of the draft. Carr led LA in scoring with 19 in his summer league debut, then came back with 26 and 8, and suddenly everyone remembered the Baylor tape. He's a smooth 6-6 wing who scores at three levels and doesn't need the offense run through him to be effective, which is exactly what fits next to stars in LA. The question is defensive consistency and adding weight to his frame. His price in dynasty drafts hasn't caught up to his situation yet. It will.
bennett-stirtz: Stirtz headlined the returnee class, an older guard who dominated his college role, and OKC at sixteen is both the best and worst thing that could happen to him. Best because the development machine there is real. Worst because breaking into that rotation is brutal, and through summer league the three ball came in at a modest clip, which is the exact skill that decides his path. High-feel, low-mistake lead guard who defends. In dynasty he's a patience play whose value is tied to the jumper falling.
ebuka-okorie: Okorie's summer league line reads like a typo: 20 points with two steals in the opener, then 14 points, six assists and seven steals in game two. Seven. The Pistons got a 6-2 pest who turns defense into offense and plays way bigger than his measurements. The concerns are the ones that come with the size, finishing over length and shooting it consistently enough that teams can't sag off. Category-league managers should be paying close attention, because steals at this volume are the scarcest stat in fantasy.
allen-graves: Graves is a 6-9 forward out of Santa Clara who does a bit of everything and nothing loudly, which is exactly the profile Toronto has turned into real players over and over. He rebounds his position, moves the ball, and competes defensively across two spots. The development points are clear: the three-point shot needs to become a weapon instead of a suggestion, and he has to add strength for the NBA glass. Deep-league stash with a multi-year runway in the right development system.
tyran-stokes: The presumptive number one for 2027 and the best pure talent in the class. Stokes is a downhill freight train on the wing, an elite athlete who lives in transition and gets to the rim whenever he decides to. The comparisons to last year's big three come with an asterisk, because the questions are real: the jumper is unproven and the decision-making runs hot and cold. That's also why he's the most valuable stash in dynasty right now. If the shot comes around at Kansas, the debate ends.
caleb-holt: Holt is the definition of positional size at 6-5 with a defense-first mentality, and he should make an impact at Arizona from opening night. He guards the other team's best perimeter player, gets downhill with force, and plays an unselfish, connective style that translates anywhere. The swing skill is the three ball. Scouts are open about it: if the shooting comes, he's a top-three pick and a two-way fantasy asset. Even if it lags, the floor is high because everything else already works.
jordan-smith-jr: Smith is the kind of competitor who decides games without needing 20 shots to do it. Two-way guard, always in the play, defends bigger than his size and gets downhill in a straight line. Arkansas will let him play through everything as a freshman. The development points are the pull-up game and adding strength so his finishing holds up against college length. Dynasty-wise he's a name to get in on early, because guys with his motor tend to out-produce their scouting reports.
cameron-williams: A mobile 6-11 big heading to Duke with the kind of frame and fluidity that gets front offices dreaming. Williams runs like a wing, protects the rim, and has flashed touch out to the arc, which is the whole modern-big starter kit. He's still more tools than polish. Strength and feel are the gaps, and young bigs tend to take longer than young guards, so price the timeline honestly. As a long-hold asset the upside is top-five pick if the flashes become habits.
anthony-thompson: Thompson is an athletic wing who scores in the ways that don't slump: transition, cuts, offensive boards and free throws. Ohio State should give him real usage as a freshman, and his physical tools alone will win him matchups at the college level. The jumper is the obvious project, both the mechanics and the confidence to take them. Wings who defend and finish always find NBA roles, so the floor is solid. The shooting decides whether he's a role player or a riser come draft season.
bruce-branch: Branch is a big wing shot-maker following the Dybantsa path to BYU, and the offensive package is legitimately advanced. He can shoot off movement, punish switches in the mid-post, and create his own look late in the clock. What scouts want to see is the other end, because the defensive effort and awareness come and go. BYU will feature him heavily, so the counting stats should be loud. If the two-way consistency shows up, he climbs boards fast.
braylon-mullins: Mullins might be the best pure shooter in the class, a movement sniper in the UConn machine that has been turning guys exactly like him into pros. He sprints off screens, his release is instant, and the gravity he creates makes an offense hum even when he's not scoring. The questions are on-ball creation and whether he can hold up defensively against quicker guards. Shooting at his level always gets drafted. In fantasy terms he's a specialist asset whose value spikes in the right system.
stefan-joksimovic: Joksimović is the class's premier international asset, running point for Baskonia against grown men while his draft classmates play college freshmen. The pick-and-roll craft is already pro-level, all pace and angles and manipulation. What the NBA will test is his athleticism, because he doesn't blow by anybody and defenses will hunt him on the other end. Euro guards with his feel tend to outplay their tools. Roster construction note for dynasty: there's always a chance of a stash year overseas, so plan accordingly.
baba-oladotun: One of the youngest players in the class and one of the longest, Oladotun is pure projection in the best sense. He's a smooth scoring wing with a frame that should keep adding function, and Maryland gets him early in his development curve. Be honest about the timeline: he needs strength, reps and consistency, and there will be freshman nights where he looks his age. That's exactly when dynasty managers with patience make their money. High-variance asset, top-five outcome in range.
brandon-mccoy-jr: McCoy is a big two-way lead guard heading to Michigan, and the defensive end is already his calling card. He pressures the ball, plays passing lanes, and his size lets him switch across three spots, which is exactly what NBA teams draft in bulk. Offensively he's a downhill driver and willing passer whose jumper remains the swing skill. Guards who defend like this always carve out careers. The shooting decides whether it's a starter's career or a stopper's. Solid early-stash asset.
beckham-black: The number one name in the 2027 high school class, a 6-3 point guard out of Duncanville, Texas running the show at Southeastern Prep. Fair warning on anyone this far out: you're drafting the ranking as much as the player, and rankings this early move. That said, the top spot in a class is the single stickiest ranking in the sport. As a deep-stash asset, being first in line two drafts out is exactly the lottery ticket you want.
demarcus-henry: A wing at AZ Compass Prep sitting second in the 2027 class, and prep wings at powerhouse programs are historically the safest archetype at this range. The scouting book on high schoolers is written in pencil, so hold your conviction loosely. What matters for dynasty purposes is simple: he's a top-three name with two full seasons of national exposure ahead to grow the profile. Watchlist asset with first-round equity already priced in.
cj-rosser: Black's teammate at Southeastern Prep and the third name in the 2027 class, a power forward on a roster that will be on national broadcasts all winter. Playing next to the class's top point guard cuts both ways for evaluators, easier looks but shared spotlight. Frontcourt prospects this young are the highest-variance bets in dynasty, so size the investment accordingly. The rank says the upside is real.
adan-diggs: A shooting guard out of Millenium High School holding down fourth in the 2027 class. Guards ranked this high this early usually got there by putting the ball in the basket, and scoring travels better than any other skill as competition levels rise. Two drafts out is where patient dynasty managers quietly build their edge. If the name climbs this winter, the price never comes back down.
malachi-jordan: Prolific Prep keeps producing pros, and Jordan is their latest headline act, a wing ranked fifth in the 2027 class. The program pedigree matters at this range: prep factories mean elite competition daily and film evaluators actually trust. Nothing about a fifteen-year-old's game is settled, which is exactly why the entry price on a name like this is the cheapest it will ever be.
aj-williams: Top of the 2028 high school class, a 6-6, 215-pound wing from Hampton, Georgia who already carries a college-ready frame. Three drafts out, the honest pitch is this: number one names in a class hold their value better than any other pick this age, and physically mature wings tend to survive re-rankings. Deep-league stash territory, but if your league rosters players this far out, he's the first name on the board.
yann-kamagate: A legitimate 7-footer out of Saint Francis in La Cañada, second in the 2028 class. Bigs this young are boom-or-bust by nature, so treat the ranking as a starting point, not a verdict. What you're buying at this range is rare physical inventory. Seven feet with a top-five class ranking three drafts out is the kind of asset that either triples in value or quietly disappears. Size the bet like it.
colton-hiller: A wiry 6-6 wing who put Coatesville, Pennsylvania on the recruiting map, third in the 2028 class at just 170 pounds. The frame tells you the timeline: there's a multi-year strength project between now and draft night, and the ranking will breathe with it. Public-school kids who rank this high without prep-circuit polish often have the most room left to grow. Long-view stash.
bamba-touray: Another 7-footer in the 2028 class, fourth-ranked and playing at Prolific Prep, which means his development happens against the best teenage frontcourts in the country every day. Two seven-footers in one class's top five is unusual inventory. The prep program will get him reps and film that public-school bigs never get. High-variance, high-reward stash with the best possible development address.
erick-dampier-jr: The bloodline bet of the 2028 class. Dampier Jr. is a 6-9, 220-pound big out of Mississippi ranked fifth, and yes, that's the son of the longtime NBA center. Legacy prospects come with a real, measurable edge: pro-level training, pro-level expectations, and a shortcut past the development mistakes that sink teenage bigs. The frame is already NBA-adjacent. Names like this tend to stick in the lottery conversation.
jj-crawford: The earliest of early calls: Crawford tops the 2029 class, a 6-5 guard out of Rainier Beach in Seattle, a program with serious NBA lineage. Four drafts out, rankings are more genealogy than scouting, so treat this as a name to know rather than a verdict to trust. In the deepest dynasty formats, the top name in a class is always worth the roster spot. Everyone else can just enjoy the watchlist.
draydne-mcdaniel: Second in the 2029 class and already at Prolific Prep as a 6-7, 205-pound wing, which is a grown man's frame for his age. That combination, elite prep program plus early physical maturity, is what lets a ranking this early actually mean something. He'll have four years of national film before draft night. Watchlist name with the right measurables and the right address.
rj-evans: A 6-7 wing out of Tampa ranked third in the 2029 class at a slender 172 pounds. The scouting report at this age is mostly projection: length, fluidity, and room on the frame to build an NBA body. Rankings four years out are written in sand, but wings with this size profile keep showing up in lotteries. One for the watchlist, not yet the roster.
cayden-gaskins: Fourth in the 2029 class, a 6-7 forward at Christopher Columbus High in Miami, the program that has churned out lottery names in recent classes. Being the next man up at a school like that guarantees exposure, which is half the battle for a ranking this early. Frame and program both check out. File the name and revisit every winter.
david-johnson: Oak Hill Academy has been stamping future pros for four decades, and Johnson is their entry in the 2029 class top five, a 6-7 forward from tiny Mouth of Wilson, Virginia. An Oak Hill co-sign this early is meaningful pedigree all by itself. Everything else is projection at this range. Watchlist asset whose next two seasons of film will do the talking.
